ref.title: The efficacy and safety of short-acting, full agonist opioids for symptom management of opioid withdrawal

sources.title: The efficacy and safety of short-acting, full agonist opioids for symptom management of opioid withdrawal
money: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

findings.quote: Opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) is a significant barrier to treatment engagement and retention for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). OWS occurs following the abrupt or gradual cessation of opioid receptor activity after weeks to months of agonism, resulting in distressing symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle pain, anxiety, and intense cravings.
findings.text: Opioid withdrawal syndrome causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle pain, anxiety, and intense cravings.

findings.quote: In response to these challenges, the use of short‑acting full‑agonist opioids (SAFAOs) have been proposed to alleviate withdrawal symptoms.
findings.text: Short‑acting full‑agonist opioids are proposed to alleviate opioid withdrawal symptoms.

findings.quote: Our results suggest that in‑hospital use of SAFAOs has the potential to improve withdrawal symptoms and reduce the risk for patient‑initiated discharges.
findings.text: In‑hospital use of short‑acting full‑agonist opioids can improve withdrawal symptoms and reduce patient‑initiated discharges.

limits.quote: However, the clinical adoption of SAFAOs remains inconsistent due to remaining concerns over their misuse potential, the absence of standardized dosing protocols, and ongoing debates regarding their safety.
limits.text: The clinical adoption of short‑acting full‑agonist opioids is inconsistent because of concerns about misuse potential, lack of standardized dosing protocols, and safety debates.
limits.second_hand: Emerging evidence suggests that SAFAOs may also serve as a bridge to MOUD by stabilizing patients during the acute withdrawal phase.

ref.title: Opioid and benzodiazepine withdrawal syndromes in trauma ICU patients: A prospective exploratory study

sources.title: Opioid and Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Syndromes in Trauma ICU Patients: A Prospective Exploratory Study
money: Supported, in part, by Post-doctoral Master of Science in Clinical and Translational Research Program/Hispanic Clinical and Translational Research Education and Career Development Program R25MD007607 and by Puerto Rico Clinical and Translational Research Consortium (National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health U54MD007587).
The authors have disclosed that they do not have any potential conflicts of interest.

design.quote: Trauma ICU patients may require high and/or prolonged doses of opioids and/or benzodiazepines as part of their treatment. These medications may contribute to drug physical dependence, a response manifested by withdrawal syndrome. We aimed to identify risk factors, symptoms, and clinical variables associated with probable withdrawal syndrome.
design.text: A prospective exploratory study of trauma ICU patients who received opioids and/or benzodiazepines.

findings.quote: Withdrawal signs and symptoms may begin to appear within 6–12 hours for short-acting opioids (peak intensity 1–3 d) and 6–8 hours for benzodiazepine (peak in intensity 2 d).
findings.text: Withdrawal signs and symptoms for short-acting opioids may begin to appear within 6–12 hours with a peak intensity of 1–3 days.

findings.quote: Once drug dependence has developed, patients are then at risk for withdrawal syndrome (WS), a group of serious physical and psychologic symptoms that occur upon the abrupt discontinuation of these medications.
findings.text: Once drug dependence has developed, patients are at risk for withdrawal syndrome, which is a group of serious physical and psychologic symptoms occurring upon abrupt discontinuation of these medications.
